title: Knight Cube
reviewNotes: Verified the seven-piece finish after ...Nxd7, including the forced knight-cube mate and drawing alternatives. Initial eight-piece setup remains source context.
transcript: Bishop to c8 is a brilliant idea, because it seems to trap the black knight. After all, all of these squares are defended by the white knights. But, the black knight still has the d8 square. And now, it seems like black is actually the one posing the questions, since there is a pawn that is only three steps away from getting a new queen. White will probably have to give up one of the two knights for the pawn, and this is going to be a drawn endgame. Or at least you would think that. But, actually white continues with knight to f6 check. And the only legal move is the king up to a7. And then he continues with knight to d5, which forces the king to go back to e8. And at first, it seems like we're not making any progress. Is white trying to repeat moves? Well, not exactly. White can actually create a checkmate threat with knight c to b6. And the threat is to come to d7 with a bishop checkmate. But, this doesn't seem to make sense, because black can simply play knight to e5, cover the check, and now he's simply out of the woods. White can collect the pawn and accept a draw, or he can come back and give a check and accept another draw. But, you see white actually has something much better. Because, as it turns out, knight to e5 does not stop bishop to d7 check. A majestic sacrifice, giving up one of the only three pieces left we have, leaving white with only two knights against the two black knights and the extra pawn. But, incredibly, [music] this position allows us to create an absolutely unique setup. Because, after knight to c7 check, the only move for the king is to come up to e7. And now, knight to c8 creates a knight cube and a beautiful checkmate.
